item.title: That Y2K feeling: Why today's economy resembles 2000
item.description:
It was an economy bursting at the seams: robust growth powered by a tech boom, low unemployment, elevated inflation and Fed rate hikes to try to cool things down.

The big picture: That was the situation in the year 2000, and it reminds us a great deal of the conditions in 2026.

  • The worrying part, however, is this: Then, as now, there were early warning signs that the technological boom powering the good times may not last forever.
  • And indeed, the cracks that appeared in the tech sector in 2000 would spill over into a broader bear market and mild recession in 2001.
  • We're not predicting that this time. History only rhymes; it doesn't repeat. But it is a historical episode worth weighing when thinking about the range of possibilities for how things may go in 2027 and beyond — particularly this week, as the debt markets funding the AI build-out have wobbled.

Flashback: While 2001 was a nasty year for the U.S. economy — a full-fledged tech bust exacerbated by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks — the year before was pretty great by nearly every measure.

  • The unemployment rate reached a multi-decade low of 3.8% in April 2000 and closed the year at a mere 3.9%.
  • GDP rose 4.1% for the full year, powered by stunning rates of productivity growth.
  • It coincided, however, with high inflation, driven particularly by surging energy costs. The Consumer Price Index was up 3.4% over the course of the year.

Zoom in: Against that backdrop, the Alan Greenspan-led Fed felt compelled to try to cool things down, lest that inflation become more entrenched. The central bank increased rates three times that year, including a super-sized half-point in May.

  • But here's where the parallels to today get even more interesting: Greenspan's justification for rate hikes could be lifted from today's Fedspeak about the AI boom — or would be if today's central bankers shared his penchant for circumlocution.

What they're saying: The "profoundly beneficial forces driving the American economy to competitive excellence are also engendering a set of imbalances that, unless contained, threaten our continuing prosperity," Greenspan told Congress in February 2000.

  • "The problem is that the pickup in productivity tends to create even greater increases in aggregate demand than in potential aggregate supply," he said.
  • "This occurs principally because a rise in structural productivity growth has its counterpart in higher expectations for long-term corporate earnings."
  • "This, in turn, not only spurs business investment but also increases stock prices and the market value of assets held by households, creating additional purchasing power for which no additional goods or services have yet been produced."

Between the lines: He was talking about the productivity boom driven by the internet and related IT innovations of that era, but it is very much applicable to the AI boom today.

  • Yes, AI-fueled productivity could create a boost to the economy's supply potential in the future, with corresponding noninflationary growth and higher incomes.
  • But that's in the future. Right now, that potential is causing surging asset prices and rising demand for inputs to the build-out, pushing inflation higher.

Reality check: The stock market peaked in March 2000. By 2001, an all-out tech rout was underway, as much of the investment in fiber-optic cable and other internet infrastructure was ahead of its time.

  • That reversed the playing field for the Fed, as the wealth effects and an investment boom that appeared to be overheating the economy in 2000 instead dragged it down.
  • The Fed enacted a surprise half-point rate cut on Jan. 3, 2001, and would ultimately cut rates 11 times (!) in 2001.

Yes, but: Interestingly, while the tech bust hammered Americans' wealth, employment prospects and capital spending, the turn-of-the-century productivity gains continued throughout that recession and the ensuing jobless recovery.

The bottom line: Even if the AI boom drives the kinds of long-term productivity surges its proponents anticipate, there is a risk of a bumpy path ahead — and policymakers would do well to study the parallels from 26 years ago.

item.title: Warsh signals steady Fed outlook despite inflation jump
item.description:
Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday that the economy has largely performed as expected since September's rate hike, hinting that little has changed in the central bank's outlook.

Why it matters: The Fed is weighing another interest rate increase later this month as inflation heats up and the economy remains strong.

What they're saying: "Over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, referring to the Fed's September meeting.

  • Warsh, interviewed by IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva, offered no explicit signal about October: "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."
  • His remarks come just before the Fed's standard pre-meeting blackout period ahead of the Oct. 27-28 policy meeting.
  • "It's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," he said, alluding to conversations with international counterparts in Bangkok.

State of play: The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to contain inflation fueled by the Iran war.

  • Minutes showed most officials expected another hike this year, though the timing remained unclear.
  • Vice chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed president John Williams and governor Christopher Waller have signaled that the Fed could hold off in October, with Waller noting that rate hikes need not come at consecutive meetings.

Friction point: Fresh data this week showed inflation accelerated in September, with signs of price pressures extending beyond energy into services.

  • Odds of an October hike jumped to 50% from 22% after Wednesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report, before retreating to 28% Thursday afternoon, per CME FedWatch.

Between the lines: Warsh acknowledged that AI is boosting spending before its longer-term productivity benefits materialize, while investment beyond AI is also strengthening the economy.

  • Warsh said AI was contributing to a "massive investment surge" in the U.S., calling the investment boom "probably the most important thing that's happening in the global economy on the upside."
  • Warsh said AI could ultimately make economies more productive and generate greater wealth. But he said the AI transition was "likely to be a very bumpy one."

What to watch: Warsh announced that the Fed will hold the first field hearing of its productivity and jobs task force on Nov. 16 in the Bay Area, bringing together outside experts to examine how AI and other technologies are reshaping the economy.

  • The task force is one of five Warsh launched shortly after becoming Fed chairman to rethink how the central bank approaches monetary policy.

item.title: Democrats post "mind-blowing" numbers ahead of 2026 midterms
item.description:
Data: FEC, Axios research. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

If money is momentum, Democratic Senate candidates are poised for a monumental Election Day.

  • "Oh my god, holy crap," said Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) when informed of Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico's $64 million haul in the third quarter of the year. "I mean, that's a number that's mind-blowing."

Why it matters: Republicans are awash in super PAC cash, but Democrats' advantage in hard dollars reveals a yawning enthusiasm gap — the kind of energy money can't buy.

Texas

  • James Talarico (D): $64 million
  • Ken Paxton (R): $18 million

Georgia

  • Sen. Jon Ossoff (D): $33.1 million
  • Mike Collins (R): $2.8 million

Michigan

  • Abdul El-Sayed (D): $30.7 million
  • Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R): $9.7 million

Ohio

  • Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D): $23 million
  • Sen. Jon Husted (R): $5 million

Maine

  • Troy Jackson (D): $20.4 million
  • Sen. Susan Collins (R): $5.2 million

Alaska

  • Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D): $17 million
  • Sen. Dan Sullivan (R): $2 million

Iowa

  • Josh Turek (D): $13.9 million
  • Rep. Ashley Hinson (R): $3 million

North Carolina

  • Roy Cooper (D): $20 million
  • Michael Whatley (R): $2 million

Kansas

  • Adam Hamilton (D): $11 million
  • Sen. Roger Marshall (R): $800,000

Between the lines: The figures reflect FEC filings as well as totals reported by the campaigns, some of which include money raised through affiliated joint fundraising committees.

  • Even accounting for those differences, Democratic Senate candidates are dramatically outraising their Republican opponents in several of the country's most competitive races.

Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that Josh Turek raised $13.9 million (not $12 million).

item.title: Geothermal finds rare political sweet spot amid AI boom
item.description:
Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyperpolarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum.

Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI, is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale.

Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting.

  • The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah).

The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging:

  1. Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes.
  2. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers.
  3. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock.

Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar.

  • The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews.
  • Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout.

State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry.

"I don't think any of us saw in 2017 that a few years later we would be in the biggest demand power boom for electricity that we had ever experienced," said Latimer during a recent on-stage interview with Axios in an event aptly titled "The energy source nobody argues about."

  • The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously."
Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence

The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes.

  • Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats.
  • Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans.
  • Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies.

By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest.

  • The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence.
  • A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer.

Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades.

  • Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells.
  • Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups.
  • Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections.

What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium.

  • "I don't think this moment would work without above-market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said.

Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water.

  • Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity.
  • Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption.

What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Banks are pulling back as AI's massive debt pile disconnects from economic reality
item.description:
Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone.

Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality.

Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns.

  • While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period.
  • More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace.
  • Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030.

Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multiday sell-off of its stock and debt.

  • Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf.

Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue.

  • It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times.
  • Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on credit.
  • Infrastructure projects and providers are struggling: Approximately $18 billion in bank loans for an Oracle data center campus recently slid into stressed territory, while Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Firmus shelved an IPO that sought a valuation north of $30 billion.

Zoom in: The constant spending relies on the belief that compute demand will never falter — a belief that has structural cracks.

  • Reflection AI co-founder Ioannis Antonoglou told Semafor that businesses may need "a decade or two decades" to fundamentally redesign their operations around AI.
  • That's 10 to 20 years of companies slowly adopting the technology that's being built (expensively) today.

Between the lines: This creates a mismatch: Data centers and chips require enormous investment today, but the returns that could justify that spend will take years to materialize.

  • Put bluntly, there is a massive gap between AI spending and AI revenue, one that won't close for many, many years.
  • At the same time, companies that are adopting AI quickly are getting smarter about using tools more efficiently, turning to open-weight models that are less compute-intensive to cut costs.

Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears.

  • The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period.
  • But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky.

The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about.

  • The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom.
  • If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears.

  • The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period.
  • But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky.

The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about.

  • The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom.
  • If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

item.title: Trump's MAGA allies openly discuss martial law
item.description:
MAGA activists are pushing for President Trump to resort to extraordinary measures — including martial law — if they believe the midterm elections are "rigged."

Why it matters: Some of the proposals go far beyond Trump's legal authority — and there's no evidence that the elections will be rigged. But people in this orbit have close access to the president.

  • Prominent MAGA election activist Tina Peters met with Trump this month. Convicted in 2024 of crimes tied to a breach of election equipment, Peters was released this year after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence.
  • Peters and her attorney, Peter Ticktin, also visited Trump at the White House in late June.
  • Peters did not respond to attempts to contact her for comment.

Zoom in: On a Sept. 30 video call for MAGA election activists streamed on Rumble, speakers warned of widespread election security breaches they believe will occur in November — and urgently pushed for remedies.

  • Ticktin, Trump's childhood friend, said on the call "there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election."
  • "They'll probably need to be commandeering of ballots and election equipment to make sure that we can get to the bottom of it before anything further occurs," he later told Axios.
  • Gregory Stenstrom, who testified about alleged voting irregularities in Pennsylvania in 2020, said he most wanted the election paused over security concerns. Alternatively, he proposed Trump invoke the National Emergencies Act to force states to change how they run elections. Stenstrom could not be reached for comment.

Peters was also on the call. She's been promoting her own plan online since August, which calls for switching to hand-marked paper ballots and a manual recount of all votes where feasible.

  • "Her plan is secure the paper ballots and recount by hand," Ticktin said. In an interview with Colorado Public Radio, he further explained this "would eliminate whatever effect the machines have."

State of play: The streamed call is a regular feature in this activist community, drawing voices from across the country.

  • Steve Stern, the host, directs his viewers to sign up through the Republican Party to become poll workers and observers for November. Stern declined an interview request.

Reality check: "Emergency powers are not just a blank check for the president to go do whatever they want. The president still has to act within the Constitution and within statutes set by Congress," said Derek Tisler, counsel for the Brennan Center's elections and government program.

He said those legal limits include:

  • Election timing: Congress sets the date of federal elections. Trump cannot unilaterally delay the midterms.
  • Counting and voting systems: States choose their voting systems and determine how votes are counted, subject to federal law. Trump cannot mandate a nationwide hand recount or order machines replaced.
  • Emergency and martial law authority: Emergency powers do not allow Trump to override state election laws or constitutional restrictions. Martial law would not give Trump authority to seize control of election materials or override federal and state election laws.

The big picture: Skepticism about the 2020 election extends into Trump's administration, including officials now involved in election integrity.

  • Heather Honey, most known for denying the results of the 2020 election in Pennsylvania and Arizona, is now the Homeland Security Department's deputy assistant secretary for election integrity and senior advisor to the ICE Director.
  • White House adviser Peter Navarro continues to promote his own report of mass election fraud and irregularities around the 2020 election.

Between the lines: "This election did not sneak up on the administration. They've been in office for 21 months. We're 20 days away from this election, and they haven't done any of this stuff," said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research.

  • White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in a statement: "Americans deserve elections that are safe, secure, and transparent to ensure full confidence in the results. President Trump believes every legal vote must count, every election must be protected, and Americans must have complete confidence in the integrity of our elections."

item.title: "Oh, shut up": Maine Senate debate gets testy
item.description:
Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson were sparring in a testy debate Thursday night when a protester loudly interrupted them.

  • "So this is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said.
  • "Oh, shut up," Jackson shot back. "I don't even know that kid."

Why it matters: Collins and Jackson are competing in one of a handful of races that will determine the Senate majority.

  • The two have traded barbs in a series of tense debates, but this was the first time they sounded like children arguing on a playground.

Zoom in: At another point in the debate, Collins, who's been accused of not standing up to President Trump enough, was asked by a moderator to name a time when she opposed him and it changed the outcome.

  • "At one point, I had organized people to vote against Secretary Hegseth," she responded, referring to the Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's confirmation. "As you undoubtedly have read, at the very last minute one of our Republicans changed his mind. Otherwise he would've been defeated for that job."
  • Collins was talking about Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who went on to call his eventual decision to vote for Hegseth the "biggest regret of my career."
  • "So that didn't change the outcome," the moderator said.

item.title: Trump names scapegoats as Republicans sweat in Texas
item.description:
President Trump is preemptively blaming Sen. John Cornyn and Karl Rove for "doing everything possible to make it hard for Ken Paxton" to win the Texas Senate race.

Why it matters: The president is publicly spinning what would be a disaster for Republicans on election night. Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.

  • "If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove," Trump posted on Truth Social.
  • Trump won Texas by 14 points just two years ago.

What to watch: Trump's post comes the same day FEC campaign finance reports confirmed Elon Musk's efforts to help Paxton across the finish line.

  • Musk gave $158 million to the Senate GOP's main super PAC in September over two transactions, as Axios reported Thursday morning.
  • The day after each Musk donation, SLF made an equal-sized transfer to a Texas PAC— a pop-up super PAC dedicated to electing Paxton.

The big picture: A new poll this week in Texas showed Democrat James Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton, 50% to 47%.

  • Republican leaders warned Trump for months that if Paxton won the primary against Cornyn it would be cost the party far more to keep the seat.
  • Those predictions are proving true, with more than $500 million in ad spending already flowing into the Texas Senate race, according to AdImpact.
  • "Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs," Cornyn told Semafor earlier in October after audio leaked from a Paxton event in D.C.

The other side: Talarico is getting pummeled with some of that money, but he's far from defenseless. He was already on the air in August, when Paxton and Republicans were still figuring out their game plan — and who would foot the bill.

  • Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter off an army of small donors. His campaign said 97% of contributions were under $100. Talarico's fundraising prowess allowed him to raise hard dollars, which command lower ad rates.
  • "Oh my god, holy crap, I saw Talarico," Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said on Thursday. "I don't even know how you raised $64 million in a quarter. I mean, that's a number that's mind-blowing."
  • Paxton brought in $18 million.

item.title: GOP senator: Cancel Thanksgiving recess if we lose
item.description:
Sen. Bernie Moreno wants his fellow Republicans to cancel their holiday plans and jam through "everything that we could possibly get" if they lose the majorities in November's midterms.

Why it matters: Republicans couldn't muster the votes for a megabill this summer, and leadership is not confident they can now. But Moreno (R-Ohio) is calling for the GOP to make a bigger push in the event of losing power.

  • "We will do a reconciliation bill, one way or the other," Moreno — who said it is "more likely" the GOP holds the Senate — told reporters outside the Capitol on Thursday.
  • But if Republicans lose: "It'll be the 'Last Supper.' So it'll be a giant reconciliation bill where we take all the Republican priorities that we can get done."
  • "If we lose the House and the Senate, we should be here from Nov. 9 until Dec. 31 with no break at all," he said. "Like, we'll have turkeys here for Thanksgiving."

Zoom in: Conversations have been ongoing in congressional offices about what a reconciliation package might look like in the lame-duck session between the election and the new Congress next year, a source familiar with the matter tells Axios.

  • "We are working with the House and White House to develop what all is included to be able to sell to the public and our Republican colleagues when we return," Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), chair of the Budget Committee, told Axios.
  • Election outcomes won't substantively change much for frequent holdouts like Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) who are on their way out.
  • That's not to mention Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), who are appropriators and known to break from the party.

What to watch: Republicans face a long to-do list in the lame-duck, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and raising the debt ceiling.

  • Those could all be considered part of a massive reconciliation package that requires just a majority vote to pass.
  • But not everything qualifies for the reconciliation process — and big bills can cause big headaches.

Other to-do items include:

  • Passing the National Defense Authorization Act
  • Reauthorizing FISA Section 702, the warrantless wiretap authority
  • Passing the farm bill
  • Passing permitting reform
  • Confirming nominations

Between the lines: Some of the administration's top priorities are banking on the partisan-led funding maneuver of reconciliation, including Trump's sprawling Golden Dome missile defense system, autonomous weapon advancement efforts and upgrades to the F-35 fighter jet.

  • Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told attendees at an Army conference on Wednesday the Pentagon needs "a minimum" of $350 billion to "rebuild the military."

The intrigue: If Republicans lose their Senate majority, it will almost certainly be Moreno's job to try to win it back.

  • He is running for National Republican Senatorial Committee chair — so far, unopposed.

Axios Defense reporter Thomas Novelly contributed to this story.

item.title: Rubio urges Lebanon to resist Hezbollah pressure over seized explosives
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio pressed Lebanese President Joseph Aoun not to return a truckload of explosives to Hezbollah after the group tried to smuggle them into Beirut last week, according to a State Department official and another source with knowledge of their call.

Why it matters: The issue is a test case for the Lebanese government's resolve to stand up to Hezbollah and implement its policy of keeping weapons outside the control of state security forces.

Driving the news: Lebanese security forces intercepted the truck last week at a checkpoint on the highway connecting the Bekaa Valley to Beirut.

  • The truck was carrying approximately 780 kilograms of explosives, including TNT and C-4, Lebanese officials said.
  • Two suspects were arrested for transporting the shipment.

After the arrest, Hezbollah acknowledged that the explosives belonged to it but claimed they were intended for use against the Israeli military in southern Lebanon.

  • Hezbollah's opponents in Lebanon seized on the incident as further proof of the danger of the Shiite militia's weapons and its independent military activity.
  • Hezbollah and its allies in Lebanon have since pressed the government to release its two members and return the explosives to the militia.

Behind the scenes: The State Department official said Rubio urged Aoun to "hold accountable all those who ordered, financed and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question."

  • Aoun assured Rubio that the Lebanese army and security forces are fully implementing decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and ammunition, and combat smuggling, the president's office said.
  • Aoun also stressed that the judicial authorities will show no leniency toward those responsible and will enforce the laws without favoritism.
  • "No one will be released unless he is innocent," Aoun told Rubio, according to a Lebanese official.

The big picture: During the call, Rubio also raised Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law, which bans any contact with Israelis, the State Department official said.

  • The topic stemmed from a complaint filed in a Lebanese court against Nada Hamadeh Moawad, Lebanon's ambassador to the U.S., for calling her Israeli counterpart, Yechiel Leiter, after his son was wounded in a West Bank terror attack.
  • Rubio told Aoun this Lebanese law "is routinely used for politicized prosecutions that deter steps toward peace with Israel."

State of play: Israel has continued its strikes in southern Lebanon and claims it is targeting Hezbollah.

  • Aoun asked Rubio to press Israel to stop these attacks and allow farmers to access their fields without being targeted, his office said.
  • After his call with Aoun, Rubio spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though the State Department would not comment on the conversation.

What to watch: Negotiations between Israel and Lebanon have slowed down ahead of the Israeli elections.

  • The implementation of the U.S.-brokered agreement over the Israeli military's withdrawal from pilot zones in southern Lebanon is also moving slowly.
  • U.S., Lebanese and Israeli military officers are expected to meet at U.S. Central Command headquarters in Tampa, Florida, next week to discuss the implementation.

item.title: Trump sues California to prevent counting 20,000 voters' ballots
item.description:
The Trump administration is suing California and two election officials over claims that there are suspected ineligible voters who received mail-in ballots for this November's election.

Why it matters: The lawsuit is asking the court to prevent about 20,000 voters from having their ballots counted until their citizenship status is confirmed.

What they're saying: "State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release statement.

  • "If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government," Blanche said.

Zoom in: The Justice Department alleges that California is knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote in the federal elections, according to the lawsuit.

  • The lawsuit says U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and ICE's investigative arm compiled the list of potentially ineligible voters using agency data and records from the Social Security Administration and State Department.
  • But administration-created lists of potential noncitizens on the voter rolls have been found less than accurate before in Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

Zoom out: California's top election official and Los Angeles County's election chief received letters two days ago threatening "emergency action."

  • The Justice Department gave Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan a password-protected thumb drive listing more than 20,000 voters and instructed him to verify their citizenship within 48 hours, according to the department's letter and statements.
  • "Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office. Our response will be grounded in compliance with federal and state voter registration laws and procedures," Logan said in a statement on social media after the initial letter.

Friction point: Federal law restricts systematic voter roll maintenance within 90 days of a federal election — in part to prevent eligible voters from being removed shortly before voting.

  • This litigation also follows legal attempts from the federal government to get California's voter rolls, beyond public lists, which have failed in court.

The other side: "This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day," Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said in a statement.

  • "The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials — who do a damn good job defending democracy — to violate federal law."

  • "The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials — who do a damn good job defending democracy — to violate federal law."

item.title: Fired FBI agents sue Kash Patel to get jobs back
item.description:
Nine former FBI agents and intelligence personnel sued the Trump administration Thursday, alleging they were unlawfully fired for working on the investigation into President Trump's handling of classified documents.

Why it matters: The agents' bid to regain their jobs adds to a growing number of legal challenges accusing the Trump administration of retaliating against FBI personnel who investigated the president.

Driving the news: "Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the 70-page lawsuit says.

  • "As a result of their unlawful and hasty firings, Plaintiffs' investigations were not properly transferred to other FBI Special Agents or Analysts. The impact of these heedless actions on America's national security is immeasurable."
  • All nine plaintiffs are seeking their jobs back. FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and their agencies are named as defendants.

The other side: Patel said in February termination letters that the employees had "exercised poor judgment and a lack of impartiality in carrying out duties, leading to the political weaponization of the government," according to the lawsuit.

  • When reached for comment, the FBI referred Axios to a Friday post on X that said "[t]his FBI has helped deliver the most prolific reduction in violent crime in U.S. history. Who wants to join the mission?"

Zoom in: The lawsuit disputes Patel's accusations, saying none of the plaintiffs had any history of "misconduct or poor behavior while employed with the FBI."

  • None had been internally investigated for wrongdoing, nor were they given the opportunity to explain or appeal their terminations.
  • The lawsuit alleges the firings bypassed FBI policy requiring an administrative inquiry before disciplinary action.
  • The complaint also notes that "[i]n many instances, Plaintiffs' immediate supervisors expressed disbelief and regret that Plaintiffs' FBI careers had been ended."

What they're saying: "With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our country with honor and distinction," Margaret Donovan of Koskoff, Koskoff & Bieder, a firm representing some of the plaintiffs, told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "[T]hey investigated leaks of national security and defense information, thwarted threats and attacks from our enemies, and responded to critical incidents like the Boston Marathon bombing, the interdiction of Iranian weaponry intended for the Houthis, and the assassination attempt against then-candidate Donald Trump."
  • "In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and law without bias or favor."

Context: Multiple plaintiffs said they were involved in investigating Iranian intelligence threats when they lost their jobs.

  • One, Jeremy Linton, was managing "several dozen" Iranian counterintelligence cases and was fired three days before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, without an opportunity to transfer his work or convey intelligence he had received to colleagues.
  • The suit alleges this process endangered American national security.

Zoom out: Other fired FBI agents have also sued the administration, alleging they were punished for investigating alleged wrongdoing by the president.

  • In February 2025, a group sued to prohibit the administration from obtaining a list of agents who investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol riot.
  • Agents who investigated Trump's conduct during the 2020 election sued over their firings in March. Three former FBI officials filed a separate lawsuit in September 2025.

Go deeper: Kash Patel's FBI loses another top official

item.title: Trump says Fort Hood shooter's execution will not be livestreamed
item.description:
President Trump said in a Thursday Truth Social post that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by firing squad will not be live-streamed.

The big picture: The president's post walks back an idea that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pitched last week, setting off an avalanche of bipartisan condemnation.

Driving the news: "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump's post read.

  • He added, "That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose."
  • Trump noted that he thinks "streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die."
  • That seemingly included Vice President JD Vance, who said he wouldn't watch the execution.
  • House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) warned footage of the execution could become a "recruiting tool for future terrorists."

What they're saying: Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement provided to Axios that Trump and Secretary Hegseth discussed the decision ahead of the Truth Social post.

  • Parnell added: "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned."

Catch up quick: The Pentagon previously confirmed that the December execution would be streamed after Hegseth said in an interview with Real America's Voice that it would be made "public."

  • But the plan received swift pushback from Republicans and Democrats in Congress alike, as well as from clergy and survivors of the horrific 2009 attack.
  • Even though most Americans support executing Hasan, a vast majority oppose livestreaming his death by firing squad, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll out Thursday.
  • Representatives for TikTok and Newsmax told Axios their platforms wouldn't allow execution livestreams or clips, Axios' Sara Fischer reported.

Friction point: The reversal also comes after Axios' Marc Caputo reported that the president himself was privately expressing doubts about the public execution after being deluged with a chorus of negative sentiment.

  • He was initially full-throated in his approval of the idea — but it took roughly a week for the plan to crumble.

Go deeper: Hegseth's public execution plan meets the age of viral violence

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from the Pentagon.

item.title: "Mommy and daddy" play nice: Apple and Meta team up to bring open-source Muse to Macs
item.description:
Apple and Meta, whose leaders have spent years trading barbs over privacy and the future of computing, are joining forces to bring one of America's most powerful open-weight AI models to Apple's high-end Macs.

Why it matters: The collaboration marks a striking detente between two longtime Silicon Valley rivals, underscoring how the AI race is reshaping relationships across the technology industry.

  • The companies still compete over devices and the next generation of computing, but both see an opportunity in bringing powerful AI capabilities to personal computers.
  • "We're excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again," Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang told Axios.

Driving the news: Meta is releasing Muse Spark Open, a model similar to Muse Spark 1.3 that it says is the most powerful U.S.-developed open-weight AI model available.

  • Meta joins a host of Western AI companies that have released powerful open-weight systems that promise to slash AI costs, provide companies with more control and offer an alternative to the Chinese AI ecosystem.
  • Nvidia on Tuesday released updated versions of its Nemotron family of models, and U.S.-based Reflection AI and France's Mistral both released new open-source models last week.
  • As proof of Muse Spark Open's capabilities, Meta worked with Apple to make the model run locally across two or four connected Mac Studios powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips, using Apple's MLX framework.

Zoom in: The prospect of a powerful model — it has 816 billion parameters — running on Apple hardware offers a proof of concept for how companies could build their own AI systems.

  • That could give companies more alternatives to Nvidia GPUs and proprietary models from leading AI companies, potentially shifting some of the economics of AI.
  • Meta's model will be free to download, with a license allowing commercial use, and will also be available through cloud providers and developer tools.

What they're saying: Wang said the companies have been working together for several months, with Daniel Gross, a former Apple executive now at Meta, helping bring the two sides together.

  • "I think he played a really big role in kind of getting the two companies to work nicely together," Wang said in a telephone interview.

Flashback: Apple executive chairman Tim Cook and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg have repeatedly clashed over privacy and their competing business models.

  • In 2018, amid Facebook's Cambridge Analytica scandal, Cook was asked what he would do if he were Zuckerberg. "I wouldn't be in this situation," Cook replied. Zuckerberg called Cook's comments "extremely glib."
  • The rivalry intensified in 2021, when Apple introduced new privacy protections that struck at the heart of Facebook's ad business. Zuckerberg reportedly told employees that Facebook needed to "inflict pain" on Apple over the dispute, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The big picture: The AI race is making for some strange bedfellows, scrambling long-standing Silicon Valley rivalries and even bringing together political adversaries.

  • Anthropic is leasing up to $15 billion per year of computing capacity from Elon Musk's SpaceX, even as it competes with his AI company.
  • Microsoft, OpenAI's longtime partner, is investing billions in rival Anthropic and incorporating its Claude models into its own products.
  • And in Washington, progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders and MAGA strategist Steve Bannon have found common ground in calling for tougher AI safeguards and challenging the power of Big Tech.

Between the lines: The Apple-Meta collaboration doesn't mean the companies have resolved their differences, but it suggests those disagreements no longer prevent them from working together when their interests align.

  • Meta benefits from making its AI models widely available, while Apple can showcase the capabilities of its most powerful computers.
  • And because the model runs locally, Meta doesn't receive users' prompts or other information — sidestepping the privacy concerns that have long divided the companies.

"Meta has no control or visibility to any of that," Wang said of how developers use the model.

Yes, but: Making powerful AI models openly available raises concerns that bad actors could remove safeguards and use the technology for cyberattacks or biological threats.

What we're watching: Whether the collaboration marks the beginning of a broader relationship between Apple and Meta.

  • For now, Apple is helping demonstrate that Meta's AI models can run locally on its computers. A more significant step would be Apple incorporating Meta's models into Apple Intelligence, giving the Facebook parent a role in powering Apple's own AI features.

The bottom line: Wang acknowledged that Apple and Meta will continue to compete in some areas, but said that doesn't have to prevent them from working together.

  • "Where it makes sense to collaborate and partner, we want to be able to do so," he said.

item.title: The too-hot-for-comfort economy
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Data this week has all told the same story: This is a rip-roaring U.S. economy with all the inflationary pressures that might imply.

The big picture: It puts Warsh and the Fed in a difficult jam. Top officials have signaled patience in further interest rate hikes in recent weeks, but the latest data implies broader inflationary pressures than previously thought, testing that conviction.

  • There is scant evidence that price pressures are receding on their own and growing reason to fear that they are becoming more entrenched, which could compel a more aggressive rate-hiking response.

Driving the news: On Thursday the government said the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts expected. It came on the heels of a too-hot-for-comfort reading on consumer prices Wednesday.

  • Also Thursday, September retail sales notched a 0.8% rise, versus the 0.4% analysts had expected. And the August number was revised higher.
  • There were only 199,000 initial claims for unemployment benefits last week, remaining near historic lows.

Between the lines: The U.S. growth juggernaut shows no sign of diminishing — but neither do the price pressures that have bedeviled the economy for nearly five consecutive years.

  • If anything, the PPI and CPI data released this week suggest inflation is broadening, showing up in sectors well beyond energy.

State of play: In his appearance at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand Friday (11:30pm ET Thursday), Warsh has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period in advance of a policy meeting that concludes Oct. 28.

  • Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson gave rather clear signaling in the last couple of weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month.
  • Warsh faces a dilemma. If he affirms that stance in spite of the hot price data, it could raise doubts about his determination to bring inflation under control.
  • If he seems inclined to raise rates, he could seem overly reactive to a couple of economic releases, contrary to his stated goal of making the Fed less "data-point dependent."

The intrigue: Surprisingly, bond yields are down Thursday despite the hot PPI number — and a surge in yields following the CPI number Wednesday mostly reversed later in the trading session.

  • It seems to reflect a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades. With semiconductor and related stocks down, money looks to be flowing into safer Treasury securities.
  • The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after the CPI number Wednesday, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead. It was down to 4.72% Thursday morning — an astonishing move for any 24-hour period, let alone one that included hotter-than-expected inflation data.

What they're saying: "Today's September PPI report reinforces Wednesday's CPI message that inflation is turning higher and moving in the wrong direction for the Fed," Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin wrote in a note.

  • "AI continues to lend upside pressure from categories directly and indirectly tied to the buildout. Businesses seem to be passing higher costs onto customers as the proxy for margins rose heftily in September."

item.title: DOJ gave California a voter list, a 48-hour deadline — and a threat of court action
item.description:
The Trump administration is threatening emergency court action unless California officials investigate potential ineligible voters within 48 hours and set aside ballots from anyone whose citizenship they cannot verify, according to two letters sent to state officials from the Justice Department.

Why it matters: With voting already underway, President Trump's DOJ could delay ballots from eligible Californians mistakenly flagged as noncitizens and set up a court fight just three weeks before Election Day.

Driving the news: Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter sent a letter Tuesday to Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan along with a thumb drive of "likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot," according to a copy of the letter shared with Axios.

  • McCotter asks local officials to investigate their citizenship status by noon October 15. The letter did not say how many people are on the list.
  • For anyone whose status can't be confirmed, DOJ asks the officials to "segregate—not cancel" those ballots and suspend signature verification or counting of any ballots already returned.
  • DOJ also asks officials to withhold ballots from people on the list unless their citizenship has been confirmed.
  • California Secretary of State Shirley Weber received a similar letter.

Friction point: McCotter closed his letter with a threat: "If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief."

What they're saying: "This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement.

  • California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a statement that the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."
  • She added that "California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls."
  • The Los Angeles County office did not respond to request for comment.

The other side: "One must question why the Justice Department would violate its own rules about investigating elections so close to Election Day, particularly when their past claims have been full of errors," said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, in a statement.

  • Becker added that the administration could have investigated California's voter rolls long before mail-in ballots began going out Oct. 5.

The big picture: The demand escalates the administration's push to uncover suspected noncitizen voters.

  • In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin alleged more than 190,000 voters were erroneously registered in California, a claim state officials disputed.
  • ICE investigators, FBI agents and DOJ prosecutors have dedicated significant resources to ramp up the number of cases and charges against illegal voting, with about 1,600 on-going cases as of mid-September.

Yes, but: The administration's sweeping claims of mass illegal registrations and noncitizen voting have quickly deflated after inspection.

  • After alleging 16,000 illegal registrations in Nevada, a review from state election officials saw that number dwindle to potentially 185, according to the New York Times.
  • In Pennsylvania, DHS officials conceded it had varying degrees of confidence in the flags it made on about 14,000 voters, according to Votebeat.
  • DHS also claimed that New Jersey had 35,000 noncitizen voters. Gov. Mike Sherril (D-NJ) did admit to mistake registrations from a software error, but the number was a fraction of DHS' claim: about 6,600.

Flashback: There have been software errors leading to registrations problems before, particularly for people using DMV services like getting a driver's license.

  • But election experts note actual voting by noncitizens remains rare.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with the California secretary of state's statement.

  • California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a statement that the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."
  • She added that "California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls."
  • The Los Angeles County office did not respond to request for comment.

The other side: "One must question why the Justice Department would violate its own rules about investigating elections so close to Election Day, particularly when their past claims have been full of errors," said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, in a statement.

  • Becker added that the administration could have investigated California's voter rolls long before mail-in ballots began going out Oct. 5.

The big picture: The demand escalates the administration's push to uncover suspected noncitizen voters.

  • In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin alleged more than 190,000 voters were erroneously registered in California, a claim state officials disputed.
  • ICE investigators, FBI agents and DOJ prosecutors have dedicated significant resources to ramp up the number of cases and charges against illegal voting, with about 1,600 on-going cases as of mid-September.

Yes, but: The administration's sweeping claims of mass illegal registrations and noncitizen voting have quickly deflated after inspection.

  • After alleging 16,000 illegal registrations in Nevada, a review from state election officials saw that number dwindle to potentially 185, according to the New York Times.
  • In Pennsylvania, DHS officials conceded it had varying degrees of confidence in the flags it made on about 14,000 voters, according to Votebeat.
  • DHS also claimed that New Jersey had 35,000 noncitizen voters. Gov. Mike Sherril (D-NJ) did admit to mistake registrations from a software error, but the number was a fraction of DHS' claim: about 6,600.

Flashback: There have been software errors leading to registrations problems before, particularly for people using DMV services like getting a driver's license.

  • But election experts note actual voting by noncitizens remains rare.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with the California secretary of state's statement.

item.title: America's wits' end election approaches
item.description:
Data: AP-NORC; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

A trio of polls out this week carries a stark message: Americans feel disgruntled, dizzy and down on the man in the White House.

Why it matters: The vibes going into the midterms are bleak, with a large majority of voters wanting significant change. But the question remains whether those sentiments will drive them to the polls.

Driving the news: Nearly three-quarters of Americans rate the economy as only fair or poor, per a Fox News poll out Wednesday.

  • Seven in ten voters say they feel like things in the country are out of control, per a The Economist/YouGov survey conducted October 10-12.
  • And eight in ten, new AP/NORC polling found, want to see either "substantial change" or "complete and total upheaval" in how the country is run. Among Republicans, 58% share those sentiments.

Zoom out: That national angst appears to be dragging down the president's approval. Fox News found that Trump's approval rating on inflation, which picked up last month, is at a new low: 22%.

  • His overall job approval rating has also fallen to a new floor in Fox News surveys for either term: 36%.
  • Fox says that drop is largely driven by voters under 45, those with household incomes below $50,000, non-white voters and those without a college degree.

What they're saying: White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement provided to Axios that "[u]nderestimating President Trump and this administration have proven the experts and pollsters wrong every single time."

Yes, but: Polling suggests that disgruntlement doesn't necessarily translate into a wellspring of positive energy toward Democrats.

  • Far more voters say they're somewhat or very pessimistic about the Democratic Party's future (47%) than those who say they're optimistic (21%), per AP/NORC.
  • About half say they're pessimistic about Republicans' future, while around 23% say they're optimistic.

Still, Fox found that if the election were held today, 54% of voters would back the Democrat in their House district, while 45% would support the Republican — a wider lead for Dems than the prior month.

  • Plus, Fox found that Republicans have lost ground to Democrats in earning voters' trust on key issues like inflation and foreign policy.

Between the lines: Republicans know that they're playing defense in an uphill midterm battle.

  • They have flooded the airwaves in once-safe states and are pulling ads in those that look like a lost cause, Axios' Hans Nichols reports.
  • But it's not smooth sailing for Democratic leadership — they are still navigating tough races and risk welcoming a new, rebellious caucus to Washington that says it's willing to buck the party.

The bottom line: Pollsters don't have crystal balls — and whether Americans' discontent translates into a midterm upheaval will only be clear after votes are cast.

Go deeper: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters

Methodology: The AP/NORC poll was conducted October 8-12, 2026. Online and telephone interviews using landlines and cell phones were conducted with 1,119 adults — 1,070 via the web and 49 by telephone. The overall margin of sampling error is +/-3.9 percentage points.

The Econmist/YouGov poll was conducted October 10-12, 2026, with 1,403 U.S. registered voters surveyed via web-based interviews. The overall margin of sampling error is +/-3.5 percentage points.

The Fox News poll was conducted October 9-12, 2026 under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), with 1,202 registered voters nationwide. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (786) or completed the survey online by following a link received via text message (302). The overall margin of sampling error is +/-2.5 percentage points.

item.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Starlink satellite services are restored
item.description:
Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield satellite services — critical tools in its war against Russia that were unexpectedly throttled this week — have been restored to full capacity, a Ukrainian official tells Axios.

  • The official also said that Ukraine conducted a strike overnight against a Russian oil refinery — defying President Trump's demand that it stop hitting those facilities.

Why it matters: The twin developments further strained the U.S.-Ukraine relationship, as the war with Russia drags on and the Trump administration sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week by lifting sanctions on Russian oil sales.

State of play: The move angered Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky responded by calling it "a weak decision" and a "gift to Putin." Trump then called for Ukraine to elect a new president.

  • The crisis intensified this week when Elon Musk's SpaceX restricted service of Starlink — a satellite service used for defensive purposes in battle — while Starshield, a tool used for offensive war operations that is controlled by the U.S. government, was also slowed.
  • After more than a day, the services were restored. Ukraine, meanwhile, fired on a Russian oil refinery, which U.S. officials are unlikely to look kindly upon.
  • The Ukrainian official said the country resumed strikes because Russia continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, despite Trump announcing that the two sides had agreed to a ceasefire.
  • That ceasefire declaration came as a surprise to Zelensky.

The bottom line: It's still unclear to many inside the Trump administration and the Ukrainian government whether Trump ordered the satellite restrictions.

item.title: CEO confidence drops into negative territory
item.description:
Data: The Conference Board and The Business Council; Chart: Axios/Emily Peck

CEO confidence in the U.S. economy sank into negative territory earlier this month, finds a survey out Thursday morning from the Conference Board.

Why it matters: Business leaders are mind-melding with most consumers, whose opinions on the economy are now lower than during the pandemic.

  • Such sour sentiment is shaping up as a key issue in the midterms just weeks away.

Where it stands: The CEO Confidence Index fell to 46 in the most recent period, down from 52 just three months ago — any number below 50 connotes negative sentiment.

  • The nonprofit Conference Board and the Business Council surveyed 131 Fortune 500 CEOs from Sept. 21-Oct. 5.
  • The survey measures how chief executives at major public companies feel about current economic conditions and their expectations for the economy and their own industries over the next six months.

By the numbers: 41% of CEOs expected economic conditions to worsen — up from 19% in the previous quarter.

  • Executives' concerns over cybersecurity, AI and geopolitics rose significantly from three months ago.
  • 94% of CEOs cited cybersecurity threats among their top AI-related concerns.

The surge in energy prices — particularly diesel, which is crucial to companies' energy costs — also contributed to the fall in sentiment, Dana Peterson, chief economist at the Conference Board, tells Axios.

  • "All these inflationary shocks, one after the the other, is weighing down on the confidence of both CEOs and consumers," she says.

Between the lines: The key worry when CEO moods darken is the spillover into the economy, as they pull back on spending and hiring.

Reality check: Despite their dimming views, CEOs have for the most part maintained their spending plans, per the survey.

Case in point: A separate survey also out Thursday morning found that 89% of U.S. CEOs said they expected to increase headcount over the next three years as AI creates more business opportunities.

  • "As we put more AI into our processes and platforms, the capacity opens up," Tim Walsh, the CEO of KPMG, which conducted the survey, told Axios' Nathan Bomey.
  • "What you're seeing there is CEOs being really optimistic that they can actually expand their business, which is going to result in a bigger workforce for them."

The bottom line: CEOs are gloomy about the economy, but their dark mood hasn't yet translated into a meaningful pullback in investment plans.

item.title: YOLO Chuck: Schumer's final fight
item.description:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is on the cusp of leading his party to midterm victory and reclaiming his title as Senate majority leader.

  • Winning the majority isn't guaranteed. But this son of Brooklyn, who has been in public life for 52 years, is more than favored to win a secret ballot to remain Democratic leader.

Why it matters: At age 75 (76 by the time the new Congress convenes in January), Charles Ellis Schumer, an old-school pol who visits all 62 of New York's counties every year, looks poised to do what very few people do in life — go out on top.

Behind the scenes: For starters, Democratic senators aren't quietly maneuvering — or publicly positioning themselves — to take the top job, according to senior aides. You can't beat someone with no one.

  • A handful of Democratic Senate candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, haven't committed to supporting Schumer for leader. But they likely don't have the votes to stage a coup. And Schumer's super PAC is spending heavily to get them across the line.

That calculus could change if Republicans overperform expectations with a massive win, potentially triggering a serious leadership challenge.

  • Otherwise, the job is Schumer's for the asking — and he's asking. "I am running for re-election for leader. Period," he said two weeks ago.

The intrigue: The bigger question surrounding Schumer involves 2028 and whether he'd retire at the top of his game or risk an embarrassing primary loss to, perhaps, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was born in the Bronx and represents parts of the Bronx and Queens.

  • If Schumer decided to retire, he could spend his final two years in leadership, freed from the political pressures that have defined his career.

That would give Senate Republicans and President Trump an entirely new political animal to contend with: YOLO Chuck.

  • Republican YOLO senators (with nothing left to lose, since You Only Live Once) have been playing hardball with President Trump. But it's unclear how a YOLO Chuck would behave as Senate majority leader.
  • Schumer, first elected to Congress when Carter was president, has spent nearly 46 years plotting what's next.
  • Not even his closest allies know what he'll be like if he's freed from the political pressures that have defined his leadership.

Zoom out: Schumer finds himself in a position remarkably similar to that of the man he'd replace: Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

  • Both are distrusted by their parties' most vocal activists. The insults hurled at them — weak, coward, sellout — are almost interchangeable.
  • But most of the criticism comes from outside the chamber. Behind closed doors, their caucuses are expected to close ranks.

What we're watching: If Schumer takes the majority, he'd have to weigh when to confront, and when to cooperate with, a president he says is synonymous with "costs, chaos and corruption."

  • Schumer has known Trump for decades, and they have a "complicated" relationship. But he'd be facing him as the co-head of a coequal branch of government.
  • Funding the government and passing the National Defense Authorization Act are must-do pieces of legislation.
  • Schumer would have to navigate those politics with up to eight Democratic senators running for president.

Between the lines: The Senate Democratic leader would also have to coordinate with a potential House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, who has struggled to maintain discipline within his ranks.

  • In the minority, the two New York Democrats have clashed over how to confront Trump.
  • They split over Schumer's decision to help Republicans avert a government shutdown in March 2025. Progressives were furious with Schumer. House Democrats held venting sessions.
  • Tensions resurfaced this year when Schumer negotiated a short-term DHS funding deal that Jeffries refused to embrace.

The bottom line: If Schumer announces early in the next Congress that he won't seek another term as leader in 2028, Washington could find itself in an unusual position — with a term-limited president negotiating with a Senate majority leader who has nothing left to lose politically.

item.title: Gen Z and millennials are running for Congress in record numbers, but few reach November
item.description:
Gen Z and millennials have launched their biggest bid yet to remake Congress, but roughly seven in 10 were out by early September, a new report finds.

Why it matters: These two generations are struggling to clear the first hurdles of a political system that rewards experience, fundraising and established party support.

State of play: A new report from Future Caucus, a nonpartisan nonprofit that works with younger elected officials, found that a record share of this cycle's congressional candidates came from the nation's two youngest political generations.

  • The group identified 3,918 candidates who filed for Congress this cycle, 31% more than in 2024.
  • Of candidates with known or estimated ages, 36.4% were millennials or Gen Z, up from 23.4% in 2024.
  • The report counts everyone who filed and doesn't track how many were first-time candidates.

Between the lines: Many young candidates are trying to reach Congress without the political experience that helps candidates advance.

  • Just 1.7% of Gen Z candidates and 9% of millennials have served in a state legislature.
  • Among congressional challengers with age data, nearly 40% of those with state legislative experience reached the general-election stage, compared with 26.2% without it.

By the numbers: Only 21.2% of Gen Z congressional candidates remained in the race at the report's September cutoff.

  • That figure rose to 30.2% for millennials, 41.1% for Gen X and 44.5% for Baby Boomers.
  • Nearly 33% of Gen Z candidates failed to qualify for a primary ballot, compared with 18.3% of millennials and 9.4% of Gen X.
  • Incumbents averaged 59 years old, nearly nine years older than challengers.

What they're saying: "They're done waiting for somebody else to fix the problems," Future Caucus President and CEO Layla Zaidane tells Axios.

  • Zaidane said Gen Z candidates running outside the two major parties face steep hurdles: raising money, recruiting volunteers and building name recognition without party infrastructure.

Zoom in: Women make up just 17.1% of Gen Z congressional candidates, compared with 26.6% of millennials and 30.7% of Gen X.

  • Younger men withdrew or failed to qualify for the primary ballot at higher rates than women in their generations.
  • Younger candidates are disproportionately Democrats, even as President Trump's GOP competes for young voters.

Yes, but: Young candidates are scoring some wins.

  • In Colorado, 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros ousted 15-term Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette in the primary for a heavily Democratic Denver seat.
  • In Iowa, 29-year-old Republican Joe Mitchell, a former state lawmaker, captured his party's nomination for an open House seat.

item.title: America's not ready for the consequences of space warfare
item.description:
The future of war is in outer space — and the U.S. is unprepared for the fallout.

Why it matters: An outbreak of space warfare would cripple the global economy by disrupting satellites used for everything from worldwide financial transactions to maritime navigation. It would also hinder the U.S. military's ability to conduct some of its key missions on Earth.

  • The dependence on satellites is precisely what makes them tempting targets for foes.
  • China has made major advancements, such as satellites with robotic arms that could disable U.S. equipment and lasers that can blind military space sensors.
  • Russia lags behind, but U.S. officials fear it may unleash an orbital nuclear weapon that "could pose a threat to all satellites and to the space-enabled services the world depends on."

What they're saying: Todd Harrison, the American Enterprise Institute's space expert, said "we've been under the illusion" that an adversary would target only military satellites and leave civil or commercial ones alone. That's no longer the case.

  • "In a future conflict, we could very well see the civilian and commercial space infrastructure that we often take for granted ... being attacked," Harrison said. "Is the American public ready for that? I'm not sure they are."
  • "We're quickly coming to the conclusion that there's no sanctuary in space, not even in a small conflict," he added.

Threat level: Last month, U.S. officials revealed that the military had weapons in space — a bombshell admission they said was aimed at deterring adversaries.

Yes, but: Doug Loverro, a former top NASA and Pentagon space policy official, said the deterrence effect is "partially the case, but not really true."

  • China and Russia have long assumed the U.S. has had space weapons, he said. In future wars, if adversaries feel they can't gain the upper hand against the U.S. military, infrastructure like GPS could be targeted, Loverro added.

State of play: Aerospace analysts warn the nation isn't prepared if China or Russia destroys U.S. satellites. They say the defense industry lacks the critical supplies and personnel to fight back.

  • The space industry is "running hot at peak demand, yet structurally fragile beneath the surface," warned PwC and the Aerospace Industries Association in the intro to a March report — in other words, U.S. space needs are outpacing equipment supplies.
  • The U.S. also likely lacks skilled engineers needed to rebuild its space assets after a crisis, RAND researchers said.

Zoom in: The U.S. has more than 13,000 operational satellites, up from just 670 a decade ago, per AEI's Space Data Navigator. China has more than 1,400 sats — almost as many as all non-U.S. NATO countries combined.

  • Yes, but: Those numbers can be misleading. China and Russia are working to close the gap in certain fields by expanding launch cadence, growing orbital constellations and developing anti-satellite prototypes.

The bottom line: The military is preparing for space wars, but the nation isn't ready for their consequences.

  • Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation's chief director of space security and stability, said the U.S. may be "ready to start a war" but added, "I don't know that we're ready to finish a war in space."

  • The dependence on satellites is precisely what makes them tempting targets for foes.
  • China has made major advancements, such as satellites with robotic arms that could disable U.S. equipment and lasers that can blind military space sensors.
  • Russia lags behind, but U.S. officials fear it may unleash an orbital nuclear weapon that "could pose a threat to all satellites and to the space-enabled services the world depends on."
