item.title: Anthropic brings Wall Street an AI bull case
item.description:
AI companies for years have promised that smarter models would be worth the staggering cost to build them. Anthropic on Wednesday made that case in cash.

  • The company presented eye-popping financials to investors, saying it was cash flow positive in the third quarter, with revenue surging nearly 50% to $16.8 billion compared with the April-to-June period.

Why it matters: As Wall Street broadly spent the day fearing an AI bubble, Anthropic offered what investors have been desperate to see: evidence that frontier AI can be a sustainable business.

State of play: The S&P 500 fell by more than 1% for the first time in 53 sessions, while Anthropic showed off a balance sheet that promises profitable AI, sources told Axios.

Zoom in: Consider just one of the stats reported by Anthropic: The company is cash flow positive even as some of the world's most profitable companies are struggling to keep their AI spending in check.

  • For context, Google parent Alphabet, long a money-printing machine, turned free cash flow negative in its second quarter as AI infrastructure investment soared.
  • Investing gurus — especially those focused on the frothiness of companies relative to their underlying value — have long seen free cash flow as a gold standard for the long-term health of a business.
  • Anthropic, a much younger company competing in the same expensive AI race, says it was cash flow positive in the third quarter. The Anthropic figures were first reported by the Financial Times.

Yes, but: The company's blistering pace of growth appeared to slow compared with the difference between the first and second quarters, when sales more than doubled.

  • Few investors saw growth as likely to continue at that pace, especially while the company faced ferocious competition from OpenAI.

Between the lines: Anthropic's latest financial disclosures reinforce what analysts and investors have been telling Axios:

  • The company's early bets on frontier intelligence and enterprise adoption are translating into meaningful financial gains that put it on track for the largest IPO in history. Some investors expect it to reach a $2 trillion valuation.

Flashback: Anthropic's early bets on coding expertise, business customers and spending discipline have paid off.

  • Claude Code, a viral hit that brought users to Anthropic in droves, reached an estimated annualized revenue of $6 billion to $7 billion by late summer, per Bloomberg Intelligence. Customers have generally been reluctant to switch once they've adopted it, per PitchBook data.
  • Anthropic charges roughly 20% to 30% more than competing models, according to Bloomberg Intelligence, a pricing power that BI's global head of tech research Mandeep Singh views as sticky given the level of intelligence customers get from Anthropic tools.
  • Anthropic's API business generates an estimated 90% of revenue using just 58% of the computing power needed to run its models, resulting in an estimated 92% gross margin before certain expenses, per SemiAnalysis.

Reality check: Anthropic hasn't solved every financial challenge associated with the AI buildout.

  • The company still faces enormous training costs and stock-based compensation expenses, which could weigh on its underlying profitability.
  • And Anthropic faces more than $500 billion in planned infrastructure and computing spending over the next decade.
  • Its premium pricing could also face pressure from increasingly capable, cheaper open-weight models.

What we're watching: Whether Anthropic can sustain its technological and financial advantages as it expands its frontier intelligence offerings into additional niche areas beyond coding.

  • The company's total addressable market will be a critical figure in its IPO paperwork.
  • One Anthropic investor said they're eager to see how the company thinks its leading-edge intelligence can translate into breakthroughs in drug discovery and other businesses beyond software.

The bottom line: Anthropic is showing Wall Street how frontier intelligence can turn into an actual business right when investors needed some good news.

item.title: Scoop: "OG" Bill Gates returns to wage war on AI risks
item.description:
Bill Gates is gearing up to dramatically expand his AI safety push, personally leaning on business leaders and considering a major deployment of his resources, sources tell Axios.

Why it matters: The formidable, sharp-elbowed Bill Gates who built Microsoft is back, and he's directing his competitive fire toward what he has come to see as one of the most important causes of his lifetime.

  • "I can reach CEOs on this better than you can," Gates told one person he consulted on AI safety, showing an eagerness for combat that associates say is a return to "OG" form.

Driving the news: Once a voice for optimism on AI, Gates has grown dismayed by an escalation of model capabilities, alarming security incidents and what he sees as insufficient regulation, sources say.

  • As he prepared to make the case for a far more robust regulatory framework on AI, he conferred extensively with leading AI executives, researchers and safety advocates, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
  • That process led Gates to see containing AI risks as one of the most important issues he will engage with in his lifetime, the people said.

Behind the scenes: People Gates has spoken to called his advocacy a "comeback tour," an attempt to rebuild a legacy that has been tarnished by his past association with Jeffrey Epstein.

  • Gates has said he's aware that some people may dismiss his warnings due to the Epstein ties.
  • "What I did do, in some ways, was very limited, and it was motivated by my desire to raise money," Gates told Axios in August. "But ... it was a huge mistake."
  • However, Gates sees the stakes as too high to stay on the sidelines and believes his Rolodex, foundational tech credibility and wealth can do an immense amount of good.

The big picture: This crusade marks a stark evolution for Gates, moving him from a measured optimist to an urgent alarmist.

  • Just three years ago, Gates assured the public that "the risks of AI are real but manageable." He viewed the technology's disruptions as historical parallels to the introduction of the PC or the internet and argued that society would adapt.
  • By August, his outlook had darkened considerably. In a sprawling essay, Gates warned that the current trajectory was volatile.
  • He sounded the alarm in an interview with Axios, indicating that the world is dangerously unprepared for the economic and societal upheaval ahead.

Zoom in: Gates' research has convinced him to step beyond essays and media interviews, although he has yet to define the exact contours of his campaign.

  • In his August essay, Gates called for new regulatory institutions capable of coordinating AI policy, reserving some jobs for humans and taxing AI usage and robots.

The stakes of the AI race have resurrected a version of the billionaire the tech world hasn't seen in decades. In recent interviews, he's shown flashes of the acid-tongued titan who ruthlessly built Microsoft, chiding journalist Ezra Klein for asking whether any regulation is needed beyond what Klein called "normal corporate reputational management."

  • Gates sarcastically made fun of a world where lawsuits are the only form of regulation. "Say you kill 100 million people. You want to use a lawsuit? I almost can't keep a straight face."
  • It is a jarring contrast to the softer, sweater-wearing philanthropist persona he has cultivated over the past 20 years.

What's next: Gates' calls for robust regulation will put him on a collision course with the Trump administration, which has favored a lighter regulatory touch, organizing a group of top officials to police the industry through a voluntary safety pact.

  • As Gates' plans crystallize, it remains to be seen whether AI safety becomes a defining battle of his late career.

item.title: Scoop: Inside Elon Musk's massive Texas rescue mission
item.description:
Elon Musk, by far the biggest known midterm donor, is single-handedly keeping the Republican Party afloat in some of its most vital races.

  • Musk's team reached out to Republicans in late August to discuss a train wreck they all saw coming: Unless the GOP poured more money into Texas immediately, the state's Senate race could be lost in a matter of weeks.

Why it matters: That chat set in motion a massive rescue operation for Republican Ken Paxton funded substantially by Musk, who gave $158 million to the GOP in September alone.

  • Musk's rescue gave Paxton's sleepy campaign new life and showed why the world's richest person is the X factor in the push to prevent a midterm debacle for President Trump's party.

Zoom out: It also helped Republicans avoid a death-spiral scenario: that propping up Paxton in Texas would force them to drain badly needed resources from other Senate battlegrounds.

  • Instead, Musk's money allowed Republicans to flood Texas' expensive TV markets and free up cash to shore up unexpectedly competitive races in Kansas and South Carolina.

Behind the scenes: In late August, Democrat James Talarico was dominating the Texas airwaves, portraying Paxton, the state's attorney general, as one of the nation's most corrupt politicians.

  • Paxton, who isn't known as a prolific fundraiser, was dark on TV. Polling seen by Musk's team and the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) suggested his chances were sinking.

Against that backdrop, Musk's top political adviser, Chris Young, called SLF president Alex Latcham with an idea: Musk would donate $5 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC if that group raised another $5 million.

  • Latcham countered: Would Musk contribute $10 million if the pro-Paxton group raised $5 million and SLF put up another $5 million?
  • Young agreed. Within days, Republicans had mobilized $20 million to get Paxton on TV.

The intrigue: That was just the beginning. SLF and Musk's America PAC concluded that a much larger operation was needed, given the enormous cost of advertising in Texas.

  • SLF and the pro-Trump MAGA Inc. would air tens of millions of dollars in pro-Paxton ads, alongside America PAC's ongoing multimillion-dollar voter-turnout operation — the GOP's "ground game" in campaign parlance.

On Sept. 11, the day after Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas, SLF launched Texas PAC, a new super PAC devoted to supporting Paxton.

  • At a donor lunch during the convention, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) stressed the importance of holding Texas to preserve the GOP's Senate majority, while Latcham made the case for a massive financial intervention.

By the numbers: Musk, the world's richest person, contributed $158 million to SLF in September — $75 million on Sept. 9 and another $83 million on Sept. 23.

  • Musk accounted for nearly 58% of the $273 million SLF raised during the third quarter. The group ended the quarter with $155 million on hand.
  • Overall, Musk has donated $276 million to pro-GOP midterm efforts since July, the New York Times first reported.

The backstory: SLF had warned months earlier that nominating Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn would impose an enormous financial burden on Republicans.

  • Thune backed Cornyn, fearing Paxton's legal troubles and personal scandals would make him more vulnerable to Democratic attacks.
  • In a memo to donors in spring 2025, SLF projected that electing Paxton could cost $150 million to $200 million, far more than a Cornyn general election campaign would cost.
  • Paxton, a Trump loyalist, won the GOP primary after the president endorsed him.

The big picture: Musk's big splash in the midterms marks a dramatic return to Republican politics after his bitter falling-out with Trump last year.

  • Musk and Trump subsequently reconciled, and the billionaire resumed donating to Republican causes in December.
  • Thune visited Musk's Tesla factory in Austin, Texas, last year to discuss the political landscape. Musk listened but made no commitments.
  • The two remained on good terms, even as Musk pushed for passage of Trump's SAVE Act, which Republicans had been unable to get through the Senate.

item.title: Scoop: The FTC demanded documents from AI giants over recent safety incidents
item.description:
The Federal Trade Commission on Wednesday sent civil subpoenas to AI giants seeking documents about safety incidents that have spiraled into an industry crisis.

  • The FTC sought documents from Anthropic and OpenAI in a probe focused on potential consumer protection violations, a person familiar told Axios.

Why it matters: The investigation is one of a number of steps the administration has taken to show a firm hand with AI companies after multiple incidents in which unreleased models hacked websites or took deceptive or aggressive steps in testing.

State of play: The agency on Wednesday sent out civil investigative demands, which help the government gather evidence and investigate ahead of potential litigation.

  • They are more than 50 pages long each and ask for documents concerning security incidents and safeguarding practices. The agency is also asking for marketing materials and documents detailing company privacy policies, the source said.
  • Investigative demands will be sent to third-party AI organizations at a later date, the person familiar said.

What they're saying: "As we improve our models and they increasingly help people in their day-to-day lives, safety remains a top priority," an OpenAI spokesperson said. "We will engage constructively with the FTC."

Zoom in: The FTC plans to compel top AI executives to testify about their products, according to the source.

  • The agency has investigative authority to examine actions related to consumer harms that could be seen as unfair or deceptive. Those can relate to a wide range of misbehavior, including how companies charge for services or if they're alleged to have misled users.
  • AI companies continue to face scrutiny about the safety of their products. FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson has echoed the view of other administration figures and executives that AI systems shouldn't be released if they aren't safe.
  • OpenAI faces a litany of lawsuits. A group of state attorneys general on Wednesday sued OpenAI under consumer protection laws for allegedly misleading users, including children, on the safety of its chatbot.

The big picture: The Trump administration has taken on a more aggressive posture toward AI companies as safety incident disclosures continue.

  • President Trump's newly minted Super Intelligence Force, which Ferguson co-chairs, last week responded to the "fraudulent" use of government systems by Anthropic's AI by announcing an industry-wide mandate to immediately notify and remediate when incidents occur.
  • The SI Force is set to meet on Thursday, sources familiar said.

item.title: Unexpected House battles pop up deep in Trump country
item.description:
Republicans who haven't faced serious reelection fights in years are suddenly campaigning like they're running in swing districts.

Why it matters: Democrats are eyeing House districts so Republican that they weren't even on the party's radar at the start of the 2026 midterm election cycle.

  • That includes incumbents like Reps. John McGuire (R-Va.) and Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), neither of whom were seen as remotely vulnerable coming into the second Trump term.
  • Most of these seats haven't elected a Democrat in years or even decades and are only truly in play if the party is winning nationally by double digits. Even then, some are a stretch.
  • But candidates in Trump country say frustration with rising prices, corruption, the war in Iran and political incumbency in general have led to a sea change that could precipitate some shock results on Nov. 3.

State of play: Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Mich.) is running scathing attack ads against Democratic opponent Callie Barr, labeling her "Crooked Callie" and tying her to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib and Abdul El-Sayed.

  • That's a stark change from 2024, when Bergman defeated Barr by 21 percentage points. His ads that cycle made at most a passing reference to Barr, according to AdImpact.
  • Rep. John McGuire (R-Va.) won by 15 points in 2024, a sleepy general election with minimal spending or ads. He too is running attack ads amid a challenge from former Democratic Rep. Tom Perriello.

What we're hearing: Democrats say they are astounded by the level of anti-establishment frustration in their districts. "We're in a real race. It's unreal," Barr said in an interview, telling Axios voters regularly come to her campaign offices "just to vent their frustration" with the incumbent.

  • "I ran in '24, and I can see, in real time, the shift," she said. "I mean, look at the commercial Jack Bergman ran about me. There's a track behind it that's whispering, 'lies.'"
  • Richard Ojeda, who is running against National Republican Congressional Committee chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), told Axios his district is "ripe for the picking" because voters are "absolutely tired, they're done with this, they know they deserve better."
  • "People here are equally disgusted with everybody involved in politics ... There's an enormous appetite for change," said Don Coover, the Democrat challenging Rep. Derek Schmidt (R-Kan.).

Zoom in: Perriello, asked to compare the 2026 election cycle with the 2008 Democratic wave in which he was elected to his first stint in Congress, said Republican presidential nominee John McCain "was a very serious, credible Republican."

  • Then-Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama "was driving a wave that turned Virginia blue, but it wasn't like the bottom was dropping out on the Republican side," he told Axios.
  • "This election has the bottom dropping out on the Republican side," he said.

What they're saying: "The bottom is falling out so fast from House Republicans, they are scrambling to shore up deep red districts that the MAGA clowns cosplaying as operatives mocked us for targeting over a year ago," said Viet Shelton, a spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

  • Shelton added, "Who's laughing now?"
  • CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for House Majority PAC — House Democrats' main super PAC — told Axios: "Coming into the cycle, our strategy was to recruit stellar candidates in order to contest races deep into Trump territory — and it's paying off."
  • Warnke pointed to Democratic efforts in Texas' newly redrawn 15th District, which Trump carried by 18 points in 2024, and North Carolina's 11th District, which he noted hasn't been won by a Democrat since 2006.

Yes, but: Despite the DCCC adding many of these races to its aspirational "Districts in Play" list, neither it nor House Majority PAC has committed any money.

  • In some cases, smaller outside spenders are filling the gap: Progressive group Science Victory Fund plans to spend $200,000 on ads and phone banking in 15 strongly Republican districts, a spokesperson told Axios.
  • That includes going after Reps. French Hill (R-Ark.), Abe Hamadeh (R-Ariz.) and Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.), as well as open GOP seats in Kentucky, Nevada and South Carolina that Trump won by double digits.
  • In other races, the candidates are doing the heavy lifting: Eileen Laubacher, the Democrat running against Boebert, raised over $10 million as of June 30 compared with the Republican incumbent's $1 million.

The other side: "Democrats are doing an awful lot of celebrating before a single vote is counted, confusing a laughable target list with an election result. ... We have the stronger candidates and winning messages," NRCC Spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement.

item.title: Republicans brace for three-way leader fight if they lose
item.description:
Speaker Mike Johnson's sudden frank talk about his political future is upending the quiet maneuvering ahead of a post-election GOP leadership contest.

Why it matters: The race could become a three-way fight if Johnson follows former Speaker Nancy Pelosi's example and tries to stay in leadership if Republicans lose the majority.

  • Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) has widely been viewed as a top contender for the job — and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) did not seek a waiver to remain Judiciary chair, fueling speculation that he's preparing to run for leader.
  • Many Republicans privately worry they're going to lose and expected Johnson to step aside if the majority slips away.
  • But his new blunt and unexpected musings on his own future challenge that assumption.

Driving the news: "In the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government," Johnson told CBS News.

  • But some members aren't buying it: "Why would you want to be minority leader after speaker?" one House Republican told us, adding they would support new leadership.

One leader not taking the bait is Scalise: "There are no races that any of us need to be talking about until after the election's over," he told Axios during an in-flight interview while campaigning out west.

  • Scalise acknowledged Johnson's comments: "I think early on he said he wasn't going to play in hypotheticals, and you know, and he might have gone down that path for a minute. We're focused on holding the House, and that's where my energy is."

Between the lines: A bad enough defeat could spark calls for an entirely new leadership team, three House Republicans told us.

  • But Johnson has his defenders: "Johnson has done everything humanly possible to keep us in the majority," one House Republican told Axios.

Zoom in: Some GOP sources believe a three-way contest could split support between Johnson and Scalise, potentially benefiting Jordan.

  • Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) intends to stay in his current role and has no plans to move up the leadership ladder, he told Axios last month.
  • Emmer staying put means three candidates would compete for one job, minority leader, without a clear fallback for the two losers beyond challenging Emmer.
  • Becoming party leader requires only a majority vote by secret ballot, rather than a public vote on the House floor.

The bottom line: The jockeying frustrates some Republicans who argue they should focus only on winning in November.

  • "How sad we have members bidding for MINORITY leadership positions," one House Republican told us in a text.

item.title: ICE says no to automatic body-cams
item.description:
ICE is rejecting a Government Accountability Office recommendation for technology that automatically activates body cameras when weapons are drawn and safeguards to ensure agents record arrests, searches and detentions when required.

Why it matters: The GAO warns that ICE risks losing crucial evidence on what happened during incidents involving force amid growing distrust over agent accountability in the wake of multiple fatal ICE shootings.

The big picture: The GAO report found both CBP and ICE are struggling to manage their body-camera programs during the agencies' shifting deployment plans.

  • CBP and ICE haven't updated their camera plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively. The plans fail to account for funding changes, expanded deployment needs and pauses in camera rollouts following one of Trump's executive orders that rescinded a Biden-era federal body-camera mandate.
  • ICE's camera activation dispute is the central flashpoint in the GAO review, as DHS accepted all six other recommendations. CBP uses technology that automatically activates body cameras when officers draw firearms or turn on emergency lights, but ICE doesn't.

Zoom in: At six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed, CBP and ICE personnel said they were unsure when they had to turn on their cameras.

  • Some said camera use is "not mandated," "up to interpretation," and "has gray areas." Agents specifically reported uncertainty about whether they should record during "subpoena issuance, in-custody interviews, vehicle searches, undercover operations, and detainee transports."
  • At five sites, people said they weren't sure how to use a newer camera model.

The other side: DHS rejected the recommendation, arguing that automatic activation "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement."

  • DHS warned that accidental activation could expose sensitive interactions with informants and victims or record people engaged in protected First Amendment activities.
  • GAO pushed back, noting that DHS offered no alternative safeguards despite the risks of critical encounters going unrecorded.
  • "ICE has acquired devices to equip all ICE officers and agents nationwide with body cameras," a DHS spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement. "Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon."

Worth noting: ICE issued no written reprimands for failing to comply with camera policies from the program's launch through September 2025.

  • CBP issued just one.

The bottom line: Both CBP and ICE say their body-camera programs are meant to improve public trust, officer safety and accountability.

  • But without clear standards, the agencies can't determine whether their programs are meeting those goals, GAO found.

Go deeper: ICE says all its offices will have body cams in 60 days

Editor's note: This story has been updated with DHS comment.

item.title: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
item.description:
The rupture between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over last week's diesel deal deepened Wednesday after an Elon Musk-owned satellite system used by Ukraine unexpectedly restricted service — undercutting Ukraine's fight against Russia.

Why it matters: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded.

  • Service was partially restored Wednesday, but Ukrainian officials were still searching for answers about why the service was throttled and who was responsible.
  • The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president.
  • A senior U.S. official said the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink service constraints. But Ukrainian officials remain suspicious.

Driving the news: Ukrainian officials said SpaceX imposed the restrictions Tuesday night.

  • The system turned off, they said, when a drone exceeded 160 kph. In some cases, it disconnected when the speed went over 80 kph.
  • The Starlink restrictions came several hours after the Ukrainian military did not receive an early warning about a Russian ballistic missile attack.
  • Ukrainian officials said the U.S. has provided such alerts over the last several years as part of intelligence sharing between the countries.
  • U.S. officials pointed to a technical malfunction in the system, but Ukrainian officials suspect that it was a warning shot from the Trump administration.
  • "We had massive [Russian] attacks today, and it's a pity that we also had difficulties ... about Starlink and about intelligence and a lot of different surprises," Zelensky said at the start of a meeting in London with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. "We count on the partnership with the U.S., but we just want to be very honest and very clear and be a strong partner."

The latest: The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense said SpaceX continues to restrict Starlink to 160 kph — significantly higher than earlier but still well below its normal speeds.

  • The ministry said it remains in communication "with partners and SpaceX regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions."
  • "The situation is better than it was this morning, but 160 kph is not enough for intercepting" some Russian jet drones, a Ukrainian official added.

The intrigue: Ukrainian officials think the restrictions were imposed intentionally by SpaceX to press Ukraine to accept Trump's demand not to attack Russian oil refineries.

  • Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski wrote to Musk on X on Wednesday: "Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you."

Between the lines: Ukraine relies on two satellite systems.

  • One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones.
  • The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes.
  • Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine.

What they're saying: In a post on X, Musk did not directly address the throttling of Starlink, but he did indirectly comment on which entity would have been responsible for the limitations imposed on Ukraine.

  • "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
  • "Starlink," he added, "is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."

Behind the scenes: Zelensky's top advisers spoke with their White House counterparts Wednesday and asked whether there'd been a decision to shut down Starlink services and what could be done to fix the situation, two sources said.

  • Ukrainian officials made similar calls to the CIA and the Pentagon.
  • White House officials told the Ukrainians they don't have control over SpaceX, the sources said.
  • One of the sources said the Trump administration is going to reach out to SpaceX to figure out what happened.
  • The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: AI tools are aiding would-be spies
item.description:
AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers.

Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them.

Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI.

  • Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room.
  • OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from."

Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit.

  • Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room."
  • Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved.
  • The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded.

The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes.

  • Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in August.
  • Last year, authorities said a man used ChatGPT to help plot the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside of the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas.

Flashback: Alfozan's case has caught viral attention across news sites and social media, but it isn't the first time a tech employee has been arrested for allegedly stealing AI trade secrets.

  • In 2024, the Justice Department indicted ex-Google software engineer Linwei Ding for stealing AI technology secrets and sharing them with two Chinese companies.
  • Earlier this year, a federal jury found Ding guilty on several counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets.

Threat level: Now, AI tools are adding a new dimension to corporate espionage, potentially making it easier for less-sophisticated actors to build spying devices while giving investigators new ways to retrace their steps.

The bottom line: AI models are creating security headaches for companies not only when they break out of containment, but also when people use them to plan and carry out crimes — including espionage against their own internal workings.

Threat level: Now, AI tools are adding a new dimension to corporate espionage, potentially making it easier for less-sophisticated actors to build spying devices while giving investigators new ways to retrace their steps.

The bottom line: AI models are creating security headaches for companies not only when they break out of containment, but also when people use them to plan and carry out crimes — including espionage against their own internal workings.

item.title: Exclusive: White House probes claims of missing Kennedy Center money in "MAGA blood feud"
item.description:
President Trump has directed his White House counsel to examine explosive allegations dropped on him Friday in the Oval Office:

  • Former Trump attorney Alina Habba told the president that another one of his top advisers — former Kennedy Center leader Ric Grenell — failed to deposit a multimillion-dollar donation that her billionaire husband made to the center a year ago, according to four senior administration officials and three insiders briefed on the controversy.
  • Grenell denied the accusations as "absurd" and a "lie."
  • Habba and her husband, Turhan Mildon, declined to comment through a spokesperson.

Why it matters: The extraordinary row between the two top-tier presidential advisers and former allies provides a rare and acrimonious behind-the-scenes glimpse into the intersection of power, influence and money in Trump's Washington.

  • The total value of the contribution in question: nearly $6 million, White House sources said Habba told them.
  • A senior administration official cautioned that "these are only allegations. We don't know if they're true. This could be a misunderstanding."
  • Said another: "POTUS doesn't want to deal with this. Of course, he's concerned. But if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem."

Just a few months ago, Grenell was friends with Mildon and Habba. But he was notably absent from their $10 million wedding that was attended by Trump world officials, power brokers and luminaries last month.

  • "This is the ultimate MAGA blood feud," said one Trump world insider with knowledge of the conflict.

Zoom in: The dispute grew out of a friendship between Grenell and Mildon, sources familiar with the conflict say. The men had mutual interests in Venezuela in early 2025, immediately after Trump returned to the White House.

  • Grenell, as a Trump special envoy, was advocating for normalizing U.S. relations with Venezuela's leader at the time, Nicolas Maduro.
  • Mildon, a Turkish national, had extensive Venezuelan business interests that were threatened by Secretary of State Marco Rubio's hardline pressure campaign targeting Maduro.

The intrigue: In the spring of 2025, Grenell persuaded Mildon to include a multimillion-dollar Kennedy Center donation in a lump-sum $17.6 million payment for a business deal involving a U.S. company, Habba told the president and White House staffers, two sources said.

  • Habba's attorneys plan to give the White House documentation — reviewed by Axios — to support her allegations about Grenell soliciting a Kennedy Center donation from Mildon to go to a private company in the spring of 2025.
  • "The White House counsel has asked for documents and proof. None has come so far," a White House official said.

Grenell called the statements from Habba to Trump "Absurd. I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all. Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations."

  • When Habba initially leveled her accusations against Grenell, she said the total amount of the Kennedy Center contribution was $17 million, the sources said. But as she learned of the specifics from her husband, she said the amount of the contribution in question was $5.6 million.
  • "This has been hard to track because numbers have changed," the White House official said.

After making his alleged contribution, Mildon never checked to see if it was deposited. He believed it had been credited because he was treated like a VIP donor at the Kennedy Center, where he met Habba in late 2025 before their whirlwind romance and marriage, those sources said.

Friction point: Mildon and Habba, the sources said, discovered the issue after their business relationship frayed with Grenell, who lost an internal administration power struggle with Rubio that culminated in the U.S. seizing Maduro on Jan. 3 and taking him to New York City to face narcotics charges.

  • In June, Maduro's successor, Delcy Rodriguez, issued an order revoking one of Mildon's company contracts to operate state-owned cement plants in Venezuela, the New York Times reported Monday. A source familiar with the situation told Axios this summer that her action was partly due to the U.S. government's prodding.
  • Rodriguez then reversed herself, the Times reported, after learning of Mildon's new relationship with Habba because the Venezuelan leader believed Mildon therefore had Trump's backing.
  • Amid the Times' reporting into Mildon's contract, Habba discovered that Mildon's supposed donation never made it to the Kennedy Center, the sources said.

Inside the room: Habba then headed to the White House last Friday to tell the president about the situation.

  • "Alina hit the roof" when her husband told her that he hadn't donated the money directly to the Kennedy Center, whose records indicate that Mildon actually owed a $270,000 pledged donation.
  • There was no record of Mildon giving anything close to $5.6 million, officials said. Mildon on Tuesday paid the $270,000, records show, to the Kennedy Center.

In partial confirmation of Habba's story, Kennedy Center staff reported that late last year there was a search for Mildon's contribution — then thought to be $6 million — but that it couldn't be found, an official said.

  • But Lisa Dale, who handled finances for the Kennedy Center then, said the only record in her books connected to Mildon showed he owed $270,000. "There was nothing about $6 million," she told Axios. "I would have heard about that."

Context: Habba and Grenell trace their roots to Trump's first administration.

  • Grenell was Trump's ambassador to Germany and then his acting director of national intelligence. Habba was Trump's private attorney and briefly was U.S. attorney in New Jersey during this term.

Between the lines: The Kennedy Center has been an ongoing sore spot for Trump, beset by controversy over his efforts to put his name on the building and fundraising woes.

  • If Habba's allegations of missing money are true, it could prove particularly galling to Trump, who views the center and its fundraising personally.
  • Those who know the president's thinking say he is particularly disapproving of people who use his name or misuse positions he has given them. His dismissal Tuesday of Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle was the latest reminder of that.
  • Two top Trump world figures being engaged in such a bitter feud adds to the complexity.
  • "Nobody wants to get in the middle of Alina Habba and Ric Grenell going to war," one official said.

item.title: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters
item.description:
Data: Gallup; Chart: Axios

Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a new Gallup survey.

The big picture: Americans' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism.

By the numbers: 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments, per Gallup.

  • That's the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974.
  • The distrust cuts across party lines: 53% of Democrats, 51% of Republicans and 49% of independents trust Americans' ability to make democratic decisions.

Flashback: Trust stood at 86% in 1976 and 78% in both 2002 and 2005.

  • Trust has stayed below 60% since 2018, according to Gallup.

State of play: Americans have more trust in their local government (67%) and state government (55%) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51%).

  • The survey also found that 42% of Americans trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33% trust the news media.

Zoom out: Americans' confidence in major U.S. institutions, including Congress, the presidency and the banking system, has also fallen to historically low levels.

Methodology: Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1–17, 2026; the weighting-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 4 percentage points.

item.title: New inflation warning sign
item.description:
America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy.

Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further.

What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note.

  • The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote.

By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month.

  • Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices.
  • Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%.

The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening.

  • Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge.
  • Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs.
  • "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months.

The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest rate hike later this month. But Wednesday's inflation data swiftly revived bets that the central bank will have to act sooner than the following meeting, in December.

  • The two-year Treasury yield — particularly sensitive to Fed policy expectations — jumped roughly 12 basis points after the report.
  • Traders now see a 47% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Oct. 27–28 policy meeting, up from 22.1% yesterday (and 18% this time last week), according to CME FedWatch.

What to watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg Tuesday that rising Treasury yields could help cool the economy, potentially reducing the need for another rate hike.

  • But the inflation report complicates that argument — showing that underlying price pressures remain stubbornly elevated.
  • Instead, the report lends support to more hawkish policymakers like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who warned Monday that inflation was "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component."
  • Hammack cited tariffs, the AI investment boom and rising services prices as additional sources of price pressures.

The bottom line: For American consumers, the risk is that another bout of inflation proves harder to shake — prolonging the affordability squeeze while keeping borrowing costs elevated.

  • The squeeze is already showing up in paychecks, with inflation outpacing wage growth for six consecutive months.
  • Real average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in September and were down 0.7% from a year earlier.

item.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
item.description:
Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment.

Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter.

  • That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month.
  • The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax.

How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment.

Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January.

  • However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years.
  • The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

item.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs.

By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said.

  • That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August.
  • Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month.

Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices.

  • Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices.
  • Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August.
  • Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month.

Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country.

  • President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies.
  • Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices.

What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday.

  • The increase will take effect in January.

The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again, with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation.

  • In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices.
  • Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month.
  • New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027.

The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month.

  • Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

item.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
item.description:
Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a ... smart display?

Why it matters: Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future.

  • It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday.

Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts.

  • Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices.
  • "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios.

Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners.

  • HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4.
  • Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri.

The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets.

  • Amazon and Google have been incorporating more capabilities into their respective assistants and accompanying smart home products, efforts that were three years in the making.
  • Meanwhile, others are betting that the AI era needs new kinds of highly personal devices. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device soon, and Meta recently teased plans for Charm, a Tamagotchi-like device meant to bring its Muse assistant to the masses.

Reality check: Apple has a loyal customer base and a history of making complicated technology easier to use. But that doesn't guarantee consumers will spend more on a category that has struggled to generate sustained demand.

  • U.S. smart speaker dollar sales fell 9% in 2024 and another 7% in 2025, and smart displays fared poorly as well before rebounding somewhat this year, according to Circana.
  • "We have definitely been in a, we'll call it, an enthusiast phase or early adopters phase for quite a while now," said Circana's Gagnon.

Zoom out: Better AI doesn't necessarily mean consumers will rush to buy more smart home devices, particularly when increasingly capable AI assistants are already available on smartphones.

  • Apple could benefit from its large installed base of iPhone owners and its ability to simplify setup, but it's unclear whether those advantages will expand what has remained a niche market.
  • "The new smart home products could appeal to consumers who have previously resisted buying smart home devices because they are perceived as difficult to set up and sometimes hard to use," Ben Wood, chief analyst of CCS Insight, told Axios.

The bottom line: A decade ago, the smart home promised to change how we live. AI may finally make that possible. But Apple still has to convince consumers that the home needs another screen or speaker — not just a smarter phone.

item.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
item.description:
Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond.

Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action.

  • U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study.

Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat.

  • Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap."
  • The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next.
  • "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study.

State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models.

  • Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here."

Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions.

  • The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings.
  • Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans.

Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes.

  • Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions.
  • She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning.
  • One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a Ph.D. student in Cornell's Information Science Department.

What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions.

  • AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said.
  • That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said.

The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

item.title: Trump plays Russian roulette on eve of midterms
item.description:
President Trump is indulging his fondness for Vladimir Putin at a moment of acute political peril, forcing Republicans in the midterms to take cover as he showers Moscow with one-sided concessions.

Why it matters: With just three weeks until the election, Trump is rekindling a decade-long, scandal-scarred relationship with a dictator reviled by most Americans — including his own supporters.

Driving the news: Since speaking with Putin on Friday, Trump has embarked on a remarkable five-day campaign of diplomatic concessions and cover for Russia — sparking bipartisan blowback just as voters prepare to cast their ballots.

  • On Friday, Trump announced a deal to unleash millions of tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, easing sanctions designed to starve Moscow's war revenues.
  • On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian refineries and demanded that Kyiv replace its leader.
  • On Sunday, Trump blindsided Zelensky by declaring an immediate "energy ceasefire." Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with no apparent consequences from Washington.
  • On Monday, Trump dismissed months of intelligence-based reports that Russia was enabling Iran's war effort by supplying information about U.S. military assets.
  • On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on the diesel deal and brushed off concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia's war machine, even as GOP senators labeled it a "betrayal" and "a gift to our adversary."

Between the lines: The benefits to Russia are clear. Far less apparent is what Trump's concessions accomplish for American security, European allies or his own political fortunes.

  • For America: Energy analysts doubt the diesel deal will meaningfully ease fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war.
  • For Europe: Washington is breaking ranks with a NATO alliance confronting a historic threat environment, as Russia escalates its hybrid campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions.
  • For Republicans: With control of Congress hanging in the balance, Trump is embracing a dictator viewed unfavorably by 81% of his own 2024 voters, according to a January YouGov poll.

The big picture: Trump's warm relationship with Putin has haunted his political career since 2016, when Russia interfered in the presidential election to help him defeat Hillary Clinton.

  • From the Mueller investigation to the Helsinki summit, Trump's deference toward Putin has long divided Republicans and put him at odds with his own national security establishment.
  • A decade of investigations, scandals and Washington outrage has done little to shake that affinity. If anything, the scrutiny appears to have hardened Trump's determination to defy the foreign-policy consensus.

What they're saying: On Monday, Trump again suggested that Russia was more interested in ending the war than the country it invaded, telling reporters: "I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky."

  • "The President's diesel deal will help lower prices for farmers, truckers, and families across the nation as he simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.

The bottom line: Losing control of Congress could paralyze Trump's legislative agenda and expose his administration to years of investigations and subpoenas.

  • But as polling alarms pile up, the president appears increasingly willing to follow his raw political instincts, regardless of the consequences for Republicans fighting to keep him in power.
  • In a Truth Social post Tuesday, Trump made clear that he sees himself as personally immune from the results of the midterms, writing: "I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE."

item.title: Exclusive: AI safety money floods into political races
item.description:
Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows.

Why it matters: The safety spending points to the unusual power dynamics in the AI race, where researchers shape policy and regulation in ways that differ at times from the priorities of the companies where they work.

  • The researchers add to the advocacy and giving of an array of AI safety groups that have been well-funded for years, including from Coefficient Giving, a philanthropy with close ties to many top AI executives, especially at Anthropic.

Driving the news: AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million this cycle on Democratic and Republican races, according to new figures shared first with Axios.

  • That includes donations from researchers, such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt.
  • It also includes Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker-backed AI safety group that has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4).

The big picture: Taking AI industry money has grown complicated due to viral warnings of catastrophic AI risk from the very same industry developing it and data center NIMBYism mobilizing communities in blue and red districts alike.

  • OpenAI president Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation from Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors, in part because of an internal revolt at OpenAI.
  • Forces favoring AI acceleration — who earlier in the year appeared to favor veiled threats to pro-regulation candidates — haven't spent as much as opponents expected, and safety advocates see an opportunity to fill the void.

Zoom in: Jacob Eliosoff, who runs the cryptocurrency investment fund Calibrated Markets, said he decided to engage in political giving related to AI after he saw early fundraising and candidate advocacy from Leading the Future.

  • Eliosoff, an active participant in New York's effective altruism community, said he didn't want to see a repeat of 2024, when crypto industry funding had outsized influence on the regulatory positions of most candidates.
  • "If politicians feel like they can't say anything because there's a very deep-pocketed and ruthless political entity that's going to go after them, that motivates me to step in," Eliosoff said.

Between the lines: Eliosoff has donated to Democrats and Republicans who he says appear to be open to taking AI risks seriously and could be well positioned to pass regulation.

  • Donors told Axios they are not primarily motivated by party affiliation or specific policy positions but by fears that industry spending will silence candidates on an unpopular technology.

The other side: Leading the Future had retained more than $31 million at the end of the second quarter and has supported more than 15 Democrats and more than 25 Republicans.

  • In a statement, the group said AI regulation will need 60 votes to pass in the Senate, so anyone serious about safety "and harnessing the benefits of AI for all Americans should be focused on building a broad coalition for action."

What's next: This cycle will be a test of whether candidates who take AI industry money and oppose real regulation lose and whether that is clearly understood as a central factor in their loss, Guardrails Alliance executive director Shaunna Thomas said.

  • "Republican leadership and the Trump administration are on the other side of the majority of Americans on AI," Thomas said. "That's a very important place for Democrats to be stepping into — boldly."

Yes, but: Guardrails faces pushback from some Democrats who warn its strategy, which includes opposing some Democrats, could help elect Republicans less inclined to regulate AI.

The bottom line: Trump allies have opened a new front against Anthropic and safety advocates affiliated with the EA movement, but their political giving — as well as the insistence of AI insiders — shows that the political clout of pro-safety AI advocacy is set to grow.

item.title: Ossoff rejects 2028 buzz amid bruising night of Senate debates
item.description:
Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced.

Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected.

  • "He is running. He's going to be your DSA candidate," Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins countered, seeking to paint Ossoff as a socialist with ambitions beyond Georgia.

The big picture: Georgia was one of three battleground states hosting Senate debates Tuesday night, with candidates in Iowa and Maine also clashing over President Trump's foreign policy, the cost of living and their records in Washington.

In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online.

  • "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign — it's just three weeks, Mike — you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house?" Ossoff demanded, referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer.
  • Collins accused Ossoff of inciting threats against his family, then attacked him over campaign support from billionaire Reid Hoffman, who had ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
  • "Mike, you really want to bring up the Epstein files?" Ossoff shot back, pointing to Collins' initial vote against releasing the documents — a position he reversed after Trump changed course.

In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state.

  • Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects.
  • Democratic challenger Troy Jackson argued that Collins has spent years helping Trump advance policies that hurt Maine, only to express "concern" and claim credit for mitigating the damage.
  • In his closing statement, Jackson invoked a fatal ICE shooting in Maine to accuse Collins of enabling Trump's immigration crackdown: "Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger."

In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek squared off in a race that has Republicans on edge, as Trump's tariffs and soaring farm costs threaten their grip on a state he carried by 13 points.

  • Hinson broke with Trump over his deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel, saying she believed there were ways to lower fuel prices without empowering Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine.
  • Turek accused Hinson of helping drive Iowa toward a "second farm crisis" through her support for Trump's tariffs and votes against congressional efforts to end the Iran war.
  • Hinson said the war should end "as quickly as possible" but rejected another congressional resolution, arguing Trump and the military could bring the conflict to a close themselves.

item.title: Judge orders White House to reinstate press access until litigation concludes
item.description:
A federal judge on Tuesday ruled the Trump administration must continue to grant CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the White House grounds while the lawsuit filed by the three news organizations continues.

Why it matters: It marks a major win for the news outlets as it maintains their White House access and signals that the judge believes their legal claims could succeed on their merits.

  • Judge Timothy Kelly, an appointee of President Trump, awarded a temporary restraining order to the plaintiffs on Sept. 24 that mandated the White House reinstate the outlets' credentials for 14 days. Last week, Kelly extended that through Oct. 13.
  • The preliminary injunction preserves the outlets' access until the case is resolved, which could take weeks, months or years.

Zoom in: "Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them [to] immediately return, reinstate, and restore the White House 'hard pass' press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO that were revoked on or about September 18, 2026," Kelly's court order said.

What they're saying: In a statement, Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., attorney for CNN, MS NOW and Politico, said the ban "blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment."

  • "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound," he said. "The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this 'unconstitutional ban on the free press' for the foreseeable future."

Yes, but: The judge's ruling doesn't guarantee that the plaintiffs have access to key areas, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One.

  • The White House has continued to bar CNN and Politico journalists from press pool assignments onboard Air Force One, despite the temporary restraining order reinstating their credentials.
  • A different White House lawsuit, brought by the Associated Press, could help clarify the extent of the president's power to bar reporters from those types of spaces. That case is ongoing.

Catch up quick: The news outlets sued the White House, arguing it violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints.

  • They also argued their Fifth Amendment rights were violated as they were banned without due process.
  • The temporary restraining order and the preliminary injunction suggest the judge believes the plaintiffs have a strong case on the Fifth Amendment claims.
  • Further legal proceedings, including a potential trial, would determine whether the White House violated the outlets' First Amendment rights.

Reality check: Legal experts believe the news organizations have a strong case because of a precedent set by the 1977 Sherrill v. Knight case in which an appeals court ruled it was unconstitutional for the White House to arbitrarily revoke press credentials based on a journalist's reporting or viewpoint.

  • They point to comments President Trump made to justify the ban, including, "They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration."

What to watch: The broader White House press pool, which consists of outlets that cover the president and travel with him on rotation, has stood in solidarity with the barred outlets.

  • The White House reached out to other outlets to fill CNN and Politico's spots in the press pool, but they have refused.
  • Some outlets have indicated that they intend to continue withholding publication or distribution of images captured as part of the White House still photography pool, "until a court has the chance to hear arguments on the legal claims filed by those media organizations."

Disclosure: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN.

Editor's note: This story was updated to include a statement from an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

item.title: Mike Johnson's Latino voter problem keeps getting worse
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) needs Latino voters to stick with Republicans as they did in 2024. But new polling shows they're drifting back toward Democrats at levels not seen in years.

Why it matters: Latino voters souring on President Trump has been part of the mood music of the president's second term. Democrats hope this helps them replicate the landslide from Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The big picture: Democrats have their widest lead of the year against Republicans, 57% to 31%, on the generic congressional ballot, according to new polling from Equis Research.

  • In battleground districts, Democrats lead 62%–38% among likely Latino voters in two-way races, ahead of the party's 2022 level of 57%.
  • That's well above the 49% of Latinos who voted Democratic in 2024, but below the 67% who backed Democrats in 2018, according to Equis, a leading authority on Latino voting behavior.

Zoom in: Republicans were convinced that Trump's undeniable gains in 2024 represented the beginnings of a real realignment, but poll after poll this year has indicated that Latino voters haven't found a permanent home in the GOP.

  • In Florida, GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has addressed Trump directly in a campaign ad about his immigration crackdown.
  • The Equis survey, conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2, provides fresh evidence of Trump's declining support among Latino voters.
  • Trump's approval rating stands at just 30%, compared with 65% disapproval. That's a 35-point deficit — and a new low in Equis surveys.

Between the lines: Economic concerns — and rising gas prices — are driving much of the dissatisfaction, particularly the cost of living.

  • 76% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which 52% identify as their top issue.
  • 54% trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 33% who trust Republicans.
  • That gives Democrats a 21-point advantage on the economy, up from just 7 points in February.

The bottom line: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. The Equis survey is the latest indication they could help Democrats take back Congress.

Note: The Equis survey was conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2 via phone and text-to-web with 1,800 registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino nationally.

  • The sample was weighted to match the composition of registered voters modeled as Latino by state, gender, age, education, vote history, voter registration date, VCH score and 2024 vote recall.
